Chapter 7: The Subtle Obstacles—Doubt, Distraction, and the Lure of Comparison.
Even after years of practice, the mind always seems to find new ways to trip us up, doesn’t it? Sometimes, it’s that whisper of doubt—soft, but insistent—telling you, “You’re just not good enough.” Other times, it’s distraction, quietly pulling your attention away from what really matters. And then, there’s that all-too-familiar urge to compare yourself to others, to measure your progress with someone else’s yardstick.
Picture a student in the dojo. They watch a classmate nail a technique, and suddenly, there’s this pang of envy. The mind starts spinning: “Why can’t I do that? What am I missing?” And the more you focus on that gap, the bigger it seems to get. Sound familiar? It happens outside the dojo, too. Maybe you’re scrolling through social media, seeing one success story after another, and suddenly your own life feels kind of… lacking. Caught up in comparison, it’s so easy to lose sight of your own journey.
Here’s something to remember from the teachings of the unfettered mind: everyone’s path is different. Progress isn’t a straight shot, and mastery? It isn’t something you can measure by looking at others. The real work is simply to notice when your mind gets caught—whether it’s by doubt, by distraction, or by comparison—and gently bring yourself back to the present.
Think about a writer staring at a blank page. Suddenly, their mind is full of thoughts about other authors, about prizes and recognition. No wonder the words won’t come. But when the writer lets go of needing to measure up, and just focuses on putting words down, the flow returns. It’s the same for martial artists, parents, friends. The habit of comparison is just that—a habit. And like any habit, it can be noticed… and released.
Doubt is another frequent visitor. It creeps in when things get tough, when progress feels slow, or after a mistake. The mind starts to question, “Am I on the right path? Should I just give up?” But here’s a different way to look at it: what if doubt is actually a sign that growth is happening? Instead of seeing doubt as a stop sign, you could treat it as an invitation—to get curious, to look a little deeper, to understand yourself a bit more.
And then there’s distraction, maybe the trickiest obstacle of all. It doesn’t shout for your attention; it just slides in quietly—a wandering thought, a restless body, or that sudden urge to check your phone. The practice here is simple, but not always easy: notice when your attention drifts, and gently bring it back. Over time, your mind learns to stay, to settle, and to meet each moment with a bit more openness.
For the swordsman, this means staying focused when the pressure’s on, trusting their process, and letting go of the need to compare. For the rest of us, it might mean staying present in a tough conversation, finishing a project, or caring for someone without being pulled away by doubt or distraction. It’s all the same path, really—just noticing the mind’s habits, and returning, again and again, to what’s real in this moment.
